The '''Johnson's ''S<sub>U</sub>''-distribution''' is a four-parameter family of [[probability distribution]]s first investigated by [[Norman Lloyd Johnson|N. L. Johnson]] in 1949.<ref name="Johnson1949">{{cite journal |author-link=Norman Lloyd Johnson |last=Johnson |first=N. L. |date=1949 |title=Systems of Frequency Curves Generated by Methods of Translation|journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=36 |issue=1/2 |pages=149–176 |jstor=2332539 |doi=10.2307/2332539}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author-link=Norman Lloyd Johnson |last=Johnson |first=N. L. |date=1949 |title=Bivariate Distributions Based on Simple Translation Systems |journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=36 |issue=3/4 |pages=297–304 |jstor=2332669 |doi=10.1093/biomet/36.3-4.297}}</ref> Johnson proposed it as a transformation of the [[normal distribution]]:<ref name="Johnson1949" />

: <math>z=\gamma+\delta \sinh^{-1} \left(\frac{x-\xi}{\lambda}\right)</math>

where <math>z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)</math>.

==Generation of random variables==

Let ''U'' be a [[random variable]] that is [[uniform distribution (continuous)|uniformly distributed]] on the unit interval&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;1]. Johnson's ''S<sub>U</sub>'' random variables can be generated from ''U'' as follows:

: <math> x = \lambda \sinh\left( \frac{ \Phi^{ -1 }( U ) - \gamma }{ \delta }  \right) + \xi </math>

where Φ is the [[cumulative distribution function]] of the [[normal distribution]].

== Johnson's ''S<sub>B</sub>''-distribution ==
[[Norman Lloyd Johnson|N. L. Johnson]]<ref name="Johnson1949" /> firstly proposes the transformation :

: <math>z=\gamma+\delta \log \left(\frac{x-\xi}{\xi+\lambda-x}\right)</math>

where <math>z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)</math>.

Johnson's ''S<sub>B</sub>'' random variables can be generated from ''U'' as follows:
: <math>y={\left(1+{e}^{-\left(z-\gamma\right) /\delta }\right)}^{-1}</math>
: <math> x=\lambda y +\xi </math>

The ''S<sub>B</sub>''-distribution is convenient to Platykurtic distributions ([[Kurtosis]]).
To simulate ''S<sub>U</sub>'', sample of code for its [[Probability density function|density]] and [[Cumulative distribution function|cumulative distribution]] function is available [https://blogs.sas.com/content/iml/2020/01/20/johnson-sb-distribution.html here]

== Applications ==
Johnson's <math>S_{U}</math>-distribution has been used successfully to model asset returns for [[Investment management|portfolio management]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tsai|first=Cindy Sin-Yi|date=2011|title=The Real World is Not Normal|url=http://morningstardirect.morningstar.com/clientcomm/iss/Tsai_Real_World_Not_Normal.pdf|journal=Morningstar Alternative Investments Observer}}</ref>
This comes as a superior alternative to using the [[Normal distribution]] to model asset returns. An [[R (programming language)|R]] package, [https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=JSUparameters JSUparameters], was developed in 2021 to aid in the estimation of the parameters of the best-fitting Johnson's <math>S_{U}</math>-distribution for a given dataset. Johnson distributions are also sometimes used in [[option pricing]], so as to accommodate an observed [[volatility smile]]; see [[Johnson binomial tree]].

An alternative to the Johnson system of distributions is the [[quantile-parameterized distribution]]s (QPDs). QPDs can provide greater shape flexibility than the Johnson system. Instead of fitting moments, QPDs are typically fit to [[empirical distribution function|empirical CDF data]] with linear least squares.

Johnson's <math>S_{U}</math>-distribution is also used in the modelling of the [[invariant mass]] of some heavy [[meson]]s in the field of [[B-physics]].<ref>As an example, see: {{cite journal | doi = 10.1038/s41567-021-01394-x | author = LHCb Collaboration | title = Precise determination of the <math>{B}_{\mathrm{s}}^{0}</math>–<math>{\overline{B}}_{\mathrm{s}}^{0}</math> oscillation frequency | journal = Nature Physics | volume = 18 | year = 2022 | pages = 1-5| doi-access = free | arxiv = 2104.04421 }}</ref>
